summary: Code-Agent/RGAO reads a 5-D structural complexity vector (dependency depth, files touched, symbol count, tree depth, cross-module coupling) from a tree-sitter code index. A hand-tuned threshold classifier then picks one of four author-defined orchestration topologies (FastPath, SubAgent, MultiAgent pipeline/swarm, DeepResearch). Sub-agents carry typed contracts with six-dimensional budgets, and a structural-induction theorem shows delegated budgets never exceed the parent's under deterministic-cost assumptions. A swarm supervisor builds a per-task DAG that runs read-only roles in parallel and never parallelises writers. All §5 numbers come from a proxy harness: the headline is agreement with annotator-chosen topologies against a regex classifier (misrouting 30.1% to 8.2%), plus microbenchmarks and a 10-issue synthetic SWE set. Real SWE-bench runs are deferred.

claims.claim: RGAO reduces misrouting from 30.1% [26.4, 34.1] to 8.2% [6.1, 10.9] versus regex classification (McNemar χ²=43.6, p<10⁻⁶) on a held-out 150-task subset.
claims.evidence: §5.1. Reviewer arithmetic: neither rate is attainable as k/150 (45/150=30.0%, 12/150=8.0%). Wilson 95% CIs at n=150 would be about [23, 38] and [4.6, 13.5]; the reported widths imply n≈500-550. The maximum McNemar χ² at n=150 with those error counts is about 31-33, and χ²=43.6 is only feasible near n≈256-355. App. I says the shift probe perturbs 'the 250-instance routing evaluation set'. These statistics cannot all come from the stated 150-task held-out evaluation. The 'oracle' is annotator opinion about the right topology (κ=0.78), not the topology that actually succeeds, and the comparator is regex keyword matching.

claims.claim: Budget conservation: hierarchical contract delegation provably never exceeds parent bounds, checked statically in O(|V|+|E|).
claims.evidence: Theorem 1 with a full structural-induction proof in App. H, under A1-A3 (deterministic tool costs, bounded retrieval depth, finite action space). Under stochastic LLM costs only an expected-budget guarantee with a sketched Azuma-Hoeffding tail holds (§6). Mechanically sound, but it largely restates the invariant enforced by the tracker.

claims.claim: Code-Agent resolves 40% of a 10-issue synthetic SWE-bench set at ~6k tokens, an 8-20x reduction over unconstrained monolithic agents (50-120k tokens/task).
claims.evidence: §5.4: 4/10 synthetic issues on the proxy harness. The monolithic token range is not shown as measured on the same 10 issues in the text. Real SWE-bench Verified/Pro runs are deferred (~220 GPU-hours).

claims.claim: Sub-millisecond DAG build, linear index scaling, 0.65 µs budget checks; 5/5 compound pipelines correct at ~6k tokens.
claims.evidence: Table 1 (median ± MAD, n=20 rounds) and §5.3. The microbenchmarks are well-reported but measure overhead, not effectiveness. The pipeline check is 5 synthetic pipelines with 2 injected interventions.

patterns.note: Four author-defined topologies, a three-gate pre-execution protocol (contract exists, budget, SHA-256 handoff validation) and an intervention state machine (Skip/RetrySame/RetryDifferent/Replan/Abort) form a developer-defined workflow layer. Comparison: none on task outcomes. The only comparison is router-vs-regex agreement with annotator labels, a strawman on a proxy metric that never shows the 'right' topology produces better code than a plain loop.

The SwarmSupervisor builds a per-task DAG of contract-typed sub-agents, runs read-only roles (Researcher/Reviewer/Planner) in parallel under a fan-in lock, and never parallelises write-capable Coder/Tester contracts. Evidence is only microbenchmarks (8-45% fan-out speedup on 2-10 synthetic read-only pipelines, Fig. 5b) and 5/5 synthetic pipelines. No comparison against sequential execution or a single agent on outcomes.

Topology (not model) routing from code-structure signals. It beats a regex keyword router on agreement with human labels (strawman baseline, internally inconsistent statistics). It degrades under shift (Rust 19.6%, >5k LOC 16.8%), and the misrouting cost in task outcomes is unmeasured.

Six-dimensional contract budgets with a conservation theorem under deterministic-cost assumptions and a 0.65 µs runtime check. The claimed 8-20x token savings is not measured against baselines on the same tasks.

Hierarchical CodeIndexTree with 1-hop RepoGraph dependency expansion and a seven-signal scorer (leave-one-out ablation in App. D.3). No retrieval-quality benchmark; the only accuracy figure is query-type classification on a legacy 10-query set at 70% (App. J, Fig. 7).
Typed ⟨I,C,T,M⟩ contracts with a tool lattice and pre-execution gates; not evaluated against an ungated variant.
Argues SWE-bench Verified is contamination-suspect and defers real runs. All reported code results are on a proxy harness.

methodology.sample: 250-instance routing label set (synthesised from test-fixture task descriptions plus 50 expert-reviewed examples), reportedly split 100 tune / 150 eval; 10-issue synthetic SWE set; 5 synthetic compound pipelines; microbenchmarks on a 200-file synthetic repo.
methodology.baselines: Regex keyword classifier for routing. 'Single- and multi-agent baselines' are referenced in Fig. 4 but without per-task measured numbers in the text.
methodology.models: GPT-4o-2024-08-06 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet-2024-10-22 snapshots (App. D.4); the router itself is rule-based.
methodology.variance: Wilson CIs and McNemar tests reported for routing, but they are inconsistent with the stated n (see claims). Median ± MAD for microbenchmarks; seeds {0..4} mentioned.
methodology.ablations: Seven-signal leave-one-out for the retrieval scorer; distribution-shift probe (renamed identifiers, synonyms, Rust, >5k LOC). No ablation of topology choice on task outcomes.
methodology.contamination_controls: Avoids SWE-bench Verified on contamination grounds. The routing labels are new but authored in-house.
methodology.languages: Label set over-represents Python and small-scope tasks (App. G.2). Rust is out of grammar and degrades routing.

standards.peer_review: NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations & Datasets Track submission, under review.
standards.artifacts: Apache-2.0 code and CC-BY-4.0 routing set claimed, with reproduction commands (App. L), but the repository URL is not in the paper ('listed in the README accompanying this preprint').

biases.detail: The headline routing comparison is against a regex keyword classifier.
'Misrouting' is disagreement with annotators' chosen topology, not a measured difference in task success, so it does not show the chosen topology works better.
Reported rates, Wilson CIs and the McNemar χ² imply three different evaluation sizes, none of them the stated 150-task held-out subset. App. I also calls the eval set 250 instances.
10-issue synthetic SWE set, 5 synthetic pipelines, a 200-file synthetic repo.
The authors built the label set, adjudicated disagreements (senior author), tuned thresholds, and evaluate their own router.
Label set over-represents Python; the only non-Python probe (Rust) degrades sharply.
The 'headline contribution' is the composition of rule-based complexity routing with a budget invariant whose proof restates the tracker's enforcement rule.

coi.detail: No vendor interest. The authors ship the system and the benchmark they evaluate it on.

verdict_reason: There is no end-to-end evidence: every result comes from a proxy harness, with real SWE-bench runs deferred. The headline is agreement with annotator labels against a regex baseline, and its statistics cannot be reproduced from the stated 150-task held-out set (rates, CIs and χ² imply different sample sizes). The budget theorem is sound but holds only under deterministic costs. The design ideas are relevant, but the KB should not count this as evidence that complexity-routed topologies or swarm DAGs improve coding outcomes.
applicability: Useful to the Java multi-repo team as a design checklist, not as evidence. Three ideas transfer to a gate design and can be tested cheaply. First, choose how much orchestration to use from measured code structure (files touched, cross-module coupling, dependency depth) rather than from task wording, e.g. a single-repo, single-module change stays a plain agent loop while a change crossing repositories gets a staged plan. Second, if a task DAG is used, parallelise only read-only roles (research, review, planning) and keep writers sequential, which avoids merge conflicts across repos. Third, give delegated sub-tasks hard budgets that sum to the parent's. Before adopting any of this, the team would need to measure on its own Java tasks whether the routed topology beats one agent with the same budget, because this paper never does. Its tree-sitter signals were also tuned on Python-heavy data and degraded on an unsupported language.

conflicts_with.detail: OpenCollab measures that model-directed multi-agent topologies often do not run as declared and that pass rates can fall when they do. RGAO assumes routing more complex tasks to MultiAgent/swarm topologies is beneficial without measuring outcomes.

MSEval reports that topology choice shifts score and cost as much as model choice, with no single topology dominating. That is compatible with RGAO's premise, but RGAO's annotator-labelled 'oracle topology' assumes a single correct answer that MSEval's results do not support.
